issues.legal_issue: The constitutional definition of a ruler empowers the President to recognise a ruler and a successor to a ruler.
material_facts: The President recognised a successor as ruler after the death of the previous ruler.
The claimant argued that the constitutional provision was merely definitional and did not confer power to recognise a ruler.
issues.conclusion: The power to recognise a ruler is inherent in Article 366(22); its wording encompasses recognition of a successor and permits withdrawal of recognition when occasion arises.
issues.legal_principle: Article 366(22), including the words “for the time being is recognised by the President,” confers the recognition power; the Court relied on the text and purpose of that clause and cited no earlier cases.

predicates.constitutional_text_assigns_ruler_recogn: The constitutional text describes a ruler as a person recognised by the President.
predicates.succession_to_a_previously_recognized_ru: A person claims recognition as successor after the death of a previously recognised ruler.

issues.definition: When the constitutional text assigns recognition of rulers to the President and a succession is involved, the President has power to recognise the successor as ruler.

issues.legal_issue: The President’s recognition of a ruler is a political exercise of executive power that cannot be invalidated merely as unguided, and a recognition dispute arising from a covenant is not justiciable in court.
material_facts: The claimant challenged the recognition and argued that the power was arbitrary and unguided.
The claimant relied on the covenant and contested the committee’s authority to examine rival claims.
A committee examined the rival claims, and the claimant participated in its proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The recognition power cannot be challenged on the ground that it is unguided. A claim to recognition by virtue of a covenant is not justiciable in court under Article 363.
issues.legal_principle: Article 366(22) makes recognition an exercise of the President’s political power and a matter of personal status, rather than merely inheritance or descent. The Court applied Article 363’s bar on court interference in disputes arising out of treaties and agreements; it cited no earlier cases.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_recognition and recognition_power_is_exercised_as_political_authority and rival_claims_are_examined and recognition_claim_arises_from_a_covenant

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_recognition: A claimant asks a court to invalidate a ruler’s recognition.
predicates.recognition_power_is_exercised_as_politi: The President makes the recognition decision as an exercise of executive political authority.
predicates.rival_claims_are_examined: An appointed body examines the competing claims before the recognition decision.
predicates.recognition_claim_arises_from_a_covenant: A claimant bases the claim to recognition on a covenant or agreement.

issues.definition: When a recognition decision is challenged, is made as political authority after rival claims are examined, and the claim arises from a covenant, the power is not invalidated as unguided and the covenant-based dispute is not justiciable in court.

issues.legal_issue: A covenant guaranteeing succession preserves claims based on law or custom but does not itself establish a right to succeed to a ruler’s status.
material_facts: The claimant relied on a covenant provision guaranteeing succession according to law and custom.
The claimant asserted a right to succession based on customary rules of primogeniture.
The claimant presented the succession claim to the committee examining rival claims.
issues.conclusion: The covenant provision is not itself evidence of a custom or law establishing the claimant’s right; a claimant relying on it must establish that right based on law or custom before the appropriate authority.
issues.legal_principle: Article XIV of the covenant preserves claims to succession based on law and custom but does not prove the existence or content of either. The Court cited no earlier cases.

predicates.succession_claim_relies_on_a_covenant_gu: A claimant relies on a covenant provision that guarantees succession according to law and custom.
predicates.claimant_asserts_a_right_under_law_or_cu: A claimant asserts that law or custom entitles them to succeed.

issues.definition: When a claimant relies on a covenant guarantee and asserts a succession right under law or custom, the claimant must establish that right before the appropriate authority.

issues.legal_issue: Recognition as ruler does not itself recognise or transfer rights to private property or infringe a competing claimant’s fundamental property rights.
material_facts: The notification recognised the successor as ruler but did not state that the recognition conferred rights to the deceased ruler’s private property.
The claimant alleged that private property was handed over to the recognised ruler and asserted competing property rights, but did not establish ownership of property affected by the recognition.
The claimant did not press the contention that the privy purse was private property; the Constitution provided for its payment from the Consolidated Fund of India.
issues.conclusion: Recognition of the ruler concerned succession to the gaddi, not private property, and did not infringe the claimant’s rights under Articles 19(1)(f) or 31. Private-property succession is governed by personal law; the privy purse is not private property to which a ruler succeeds.
issues.legal_principle: Article 366(22) concerns recognition of a ruler, not succession to private property. Rights in private property depend on the personal law of succession. Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 require an established property right affected by the challenged act; Article 291 provides for payment of the privy purse from the Consolidated Fund of India, and Article 362 concerns personal rights, privileges, and dignities. The Court cited no earlier cases.

predicates.constitutional_property_rights_challenge: A claimant challenges ruler recognition as an infringement of constitutional property rights.
predicates.ruler_recognition_does_not_convey_privat: The recognition instrument identifies a ruler but does not grant or transfer private property.
predicates.claimant_does_not_establish_property_aff: The claimant fails to establish ownership of, or a right to, private property affected by the recognition.

issues.definition: When a constitutional property-rights challenge concerns recognition that does not convey private property and the claimant does not establish an affected property right, the recognition does not infringe the claimant’s fundamental property rights.
